lead: Micro sensors are built on a silicon wafer by adding thin layers and removing them in patterns. Lithography draws the pattern, etching cuts it, and deposition fills or coats it. Bulk micromachining uses a wet etch that stops on crystal planes; surface micromachining uses a sacrificial layer that is dissolved to free a structure. The process choice fixes the shape, the material and the cost. Pressure sensors, accelerometers and gas sensors in phones and cars are made this way, and every added mask adds rupees to the die.
prereq: You need silicon and oxide materials from semiconductor sensors and sensor materials, and the diaphragms and beams from MEMS micro sensors.

sections.h3: The pattern loop: lithography, etch and deposition

blocks.text: A micro-fabrication recipe is a loop. A wafer is cleaned and coated with a resist, a polymer that changes solubility when exposed to light. A mask carries the pattern. Exposure through the mask, then development, leaves resist only where the pattern needs it. The resist protects the layer below during etch, or lifts off after deposition.

Etch removes material; deposition adds it. After the loop, the resist is stripped. Each loop needs one mask, and each mask must be aligned to the previous pattern. Alignment error is a real limit, often a fraction of a micrometre. A simple sensor may use two or three masks; a complex one may use ten. Cost rises with mask count because every loop adds exposure, etch, cleaning and yield loss.

items: Clean the wafer and grow or deposit the first layer.
Align the mask, expose, and develop the resist.
Etch the open areas or deposit through them.
Strip the resist and inspect the pattern.

blocks.where: d is etch depth in micrometres (µm); r is etch rate in µm/min; t is etch time in min. For a wet etch, r depends on crystal plane, temperature and concentration.

blocks.text: Bulk micromachining removes silicon from the wafer body. KOH (potassium hydroxide) or TMAH (tetramethylammonium hydroxide) in water etches (100) silicon much faster than (111) silicon. The (111) planes therefore stop the etch and leave sidewalls at 54.7° to the surface. A pit is wider at the top than at the bottom, so the mask opening must be larger than the final diaphragm. An etch-stop layer can stop the depth: heavily boron-doped silicon etches very slowly, and a silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafer has a buried oxide that stops the etch cleanly.

Deep reactive ion etching (DRIE) is a dry process that alternates etching and polymer passivation. It gives near-vertical walls and high aspect ratio, meaning depth divided by width can be 10 or more. DRIE does not rely on crystal planes, so it can cut arbitrary shapes, but it is slower and costlier per wafer than a KOH bath.

Surface micromachining, also called the sacrificial-layer process, builds on top of the wafer. A structural layer such as polysilicon is deposited over a sacrificial oxide, patterned, and then the oxide is dissolved in hydrofluoric acid (HF). The structure is released and may be free to move. Stiction is the main failure: capillary forces during drying pull the freed beam down to the substrate and it sticks. Critical-point drying or vapour HF release reduces stiction.

LIGA (X-ray lithography and electroplating) makes tall metal parts with vertical walls. Electroplating alone can make thick nickel or copper structures for coils and moulds. As parts shrink, surface forces and thin-film stress grow in importance compared with weight, so release and drying need more care.

Thermal oxidation grows SiO<sub>2</sub> by consuming silicon at 900-1100 °C. It gives a dense, stable oxide for masks, insulation and sacrificial layers. LPCVD (low-pressure chemical vapour deposition) deposits polysilicon, silicon nitride and oxide at around 600-800 °C with good uniformity. PECVD (plasma-enhanced CVD) runs cooler, often 200-400 °C, but the film may contain hydrogen. Sputtering throws atoms from a target by plasma ions and is used for metals and piezoresistive films. Evaporation heats a source in vacuum; it is simple but throws atoms in straight lines, so step coverage is poor. Spin coating spreads a liquid resist or polymer into a thin film. Electroplating uses current to grow metal from a solution onto a seed layer.

blocks.text: After processing, the wafer is bonded to glass by anodic bonding or glass frit, diced into chips, attached to a package and sealed. Hermetic sealing keeps water vapour away from released structures. Packaging is often the largest part of the cost, and most field failures start at the package: moisture, stress and bond-wire fatigue.

The same steps make medical devices. KOH and DRIE cut silicon microneedles that pierce only the outer skin for painless drug delivery or fluid sampling; bulk-etched diaphragms become catheter-tip pressure sensors; DRIE shanks with thin-film electrodes become neural recording probes; and soft lithography, a resist mould copied into the polymer PDMS, makes the microfluidic channels of lab-on-chip blood and urine tests.

examples.question: A KOH bath at 80 °C etches the (100) plane of silicon at 1.4 µm/min and the (111) plane at 0.02 µm/min. Find the time to etch a 300 µm deep pit and the distance the (111) face recedes in that time. Comment on whether the sidewall can be treated as an etch stop.
steps: Identify the rates: r<sub>100</sub> = 1.4 µm/min for the (100) plane, r<sub>111</sub> = 0.02 µm/min for the (111) plane, and depth d = 300 µm.
Convert to hours: 214.2857 / 60 = 3.5714 h, about 3.57 h.
Compare: 4.2857 µm is about 1.4% of 300 µm, so the (111) face moves little and the sidewall is effectively an etch stop, but not perfectly zero.
examples.answer: Time = 214.2857 min (3.5714 h); the (111) face recedes 4.2857 µm, so the sidewall is effectively an etch stop but not perfectly zero.
examples.check:
depth = 300.0
r100 = 1.4
r111 = 0.02
t = depth / r100
hours = t / 60.0
rec = r111 * t
print(f"{t:.4f}")
print(f"{hours:.4f}")
print(f"{rec:.4f}")

examples.question: A pressure sensor needs a square diaphragm 1000 µm wide and 20 µm thick on a (100) wafer 525 µm thick, etched from the back in KOH at 1.4 µm/min, with an etch-stop layer that fixes the 20 µm. Find the etch depth, the etch time and the size of the square mask opening on the back face.
steps: The (111) sidewalls slope at 54.74° to the surface, so each side of the pit moves out by d / tan 54.74° = 505 × 0.7071 = 357.1 µm between the bottom and the top.
Mask opening = diaphragm width + 2 × run-out = 1000 + 2 × 357.1 = 1714 µm.

Check: the opening is 1.7 times the diaphragm, so a KOH-etched die cannot be much smaller than about 2 mm across. DRIE, with vertical walls, would need only a 1000 µm opening, which is why dense arrays use DRIE.
examples.answer: The pit is 505 µm deep and takes about 361 min (6.0 h); the back-side mask opening must be about 1714 µm square.
examples.check:
import math
d = 525 - 20
print(d)
print(round(d / 1.4, 1))
print(round(1000 + 2 * d / math.tan(math.radians(54.74))))

traps: Saying KOH gives vertical walls. KOH gives 54.7° (111) sidewalls; vertical walls need DRIE.
Confusing the sacrificial layer with the structural layer. HF removes the oxide, not the polysilicon beam.
Putting stiction during the HF etch. Stiction happens mainly during drying after release, when capillary forces pull the beam down.

Mixing etch-rate units. A rate in µm/s is 60 times smaller as a number than the same rate in µm/min, so the time you compute is in seconds and is 60 times the time in minutes. Convert every rate and time to the same units before dividing. Example: 1.4 µm/min = 0.0233 µm/s; 300 µm takes 214.3 min = 12 857 s.

quiz.q: State why (111) planes stop a KOH etch in (100) silicon.
quiz.a: KOH etches (111) silicon much more slowly than (100) silicon. The exposed (111) planes form sidewalls at 54.7° to the surface, and the etch practically stops there.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between bulk and surface micromachining.
quiz.a: Bulk micromachining removes material from the wafer body, often by a wet etch that stops on crystal planes, to make diaphragms and pits. Surface micromachining builds a structural layer on top of the wafer over a sacrificial oxide, then dissolves the oxide in HF to release the structure.

quiz.q: A DRIE step etches silicon at 3.0 µm/min. Find the time for a 250 µm deep trench.
Why does stiction occur when a released beam is dried, and name one cure.
quiz.a: As the rinse liquid evaporates, a liquid-vapour interface forms and capillary force pulls the free beam down to the substrate. If it touches, adhesion keeps it stuck. Critical-point drying or vapour HF release avoids the interface and reduces stiction.

quiz.q: Name two deposition methods and one material each.
quiz.a: LPCVD deposits polysilicon; sputtering deposits aluminium.

quiz.q: Why does an extra mask increase cost more than just the exposure time?
quiz.a: It adds resist coating, alignment, exposure, development, etch or deposition, resist strip and inspection. It also adds alignment error and a chance of yield loss, so the cost per wafer rises with every mask.

quiz.q: A KOH pit is 300 µm deep. Explain why the mask opening must be larger than the final diaphragm.
quiz.a: The (111) sidewalls slope at 54.7° to the surface, so the pit is widest at the mask opening and narrows as it goes down. The mask opening must therefore be larger than the final diaphragm by the sidewall run-out on each side, about 0.71 × depth (about 212 µm per side for a 300 µm pit); otherwise the diaphragm comes out smaller than designed.

quiz.q: If r<sub>100</sub> = 1.0 µm/min and r<sub>111</sub> = 0.01 µm/min, find the anisotropy ratio r<sub>100</sub> / r<sub>111</sub>.
quiz.a: Anisotropy ratio = 1.0 / 0.01 = 100. A high ratio means the (111) plane acts as a good etch stop.

beyond: Not for the exam. MEMS foundries give process design kits with fixed layer stacks, so designers choose from available depositions and etches rather than inventing a whole flow. The Bosch process is the common cycle of etch and passivation used in DRIE. SOI wafers with a buried oxide are widely used for clean etch stops and released structures. Search next for “Bosch process”, “anodic bonding”, “critical-point drying” and “MEMS process design kit”.
